name: Calendula extract

lead: Calendula extract comes from pot marigold flowers and is used in creams and balms to calm irritated skin so it looks less red and more comfortable. It has a long history in traditional wound-care products.

Laboratory studies report anti-inflammatory activity for flower extracts, though the mechanism in human skin is not established in the sources reviewed. A 2019 systematic review of calendula as a single wound-healing treatment covered 14 studies, 7 in animals and 7 clinical trials. No published trial listed here has tested it for appearance goals such as acne or skin aging.

paras: People use it in soothing creams, balms and toners applied to irritated or sensitive skin, usually as part of a gentle routine. It is typically one ingredient among several.
The sources reviewed do not describe significant adverse effects of topical use; safety data are limited to the small studies cited.

angle.text: Calendula extract is used to calm irritated skin so it looks less red and more even. Lab studies report anti-inflammatory activity, and human and animal studies have looked at wound healing.

lead: Calendula extract is a preparation from the flowers of Calendula officinalis, used in topical skincare and traditional wound-care products. Laboratory studies have reported anti-inflammatory properties for flower extracts,[1] and human and animal studies have examined it mainly for wound healing.[2]

A 2019 systematic review of calendula extract as a single treatment for wound healing covered 14 studies, 7 animal experiments and 7 clinical trials.[2] No published trial listed here has tested it for cosmetic appearance goals such as acne or skin aging.

paras: Calendula extract appears in topical wound-care and skincare products. Studies have also examined it in a mouthwash for radiation-induced oral mucositis.[3] One study measured effects of calendula extract on mechanical parameters of human skin.[4]

Laboratory work includes a rodent study reporting that oral flower extract reduced induced paw swelling,[1] and in vitro work on a laser-activated extract reporting cytotoxic and lymphocyte-activating effects.[5] These findings come from animal or cell models and are not evidence of appearance benefit in people. Formulation research has examined hydrogels and nanoparticles for delivery.[6]

The 2019 systematic review included seven clinical trials of calendula extract for wound healing.[2] In a randomized study of 40 head-and-neck cancer patients, a 2% calendula mouthwash was compared with placebo for radiation-induced oropharyngeal mucositis.[3] A study of calendula extract on mechanical parameters of human skin has also been published.[4] Trials focused on cosmetic skin appearance were not found among the sources reviewed.
